notes: Two self checks were lying, and they were caught by running the suite against the live copy rather than against a fresh one. 3.440.0 reported 211 of 211 on a clean browser and 209 of 211 on a tablet with a real inspection loaded. Neither failure was a fault in the app. Both tests inherited whatever job was open and then asserted something only true of an empty file: one checked that a meter the aircraft does not have is left off the owner's page, and went red on any aircraft with an engine-overhaul time entered; the other counted logbook cards after replacing the squawks, and counted the cards built from upgrades and from checklist wording too, reporting eight where it wanted one. Both now run against a blank job, which is what they always meant to do. The whole suite was then re-run against a deliberately heavy job — nine findings across three dispositions, checklist wording, a completed upgrade, an open AD, an invoice with labor, parts and a receipt, and a booked schedule — and all 211 pass. A self check that goes red on real work is worse than no check at all, because the number stops meaning anything and people start ignoring it. Everything from 3.440.0 is unchanged.
validated_against: The FAA's own model search on drs.faa.gov, 23 models, Status=Current: 693 directives listed, 693 returned, 0 wrongly set aside. Perfect on every individual model. AD Toolbox's airframe lists hold 528 of the same 693 — mostly by design, since their appliance directives sit in a separate unmatched list of 581.
reliability: 211 self checks passing on a blank job AND on a fully populated one, which is the stronger claim and the one that was not being made before. No count changed; two checks that only ever passed by accident now pass on purpose.

index.source: FAA Dynamic Regulatory System, AD Final Rules

storage: The directive index no longer shares a database with jobs and photographs. It lives in Cache Storage under 'adx-1'. Any copy left in the old place is deleted on first load. This is the second half of the 30 August fix: the database that wedged that morning is now smaller and is never touched by an AD search. From 3.390.0 the app also asks for persistent storage at startup, so a tablet's inspections are not data the browser may quietly reclaim, and it watches how full the device is — warning while there is still room to write the export that gets the job off, rather than after there is not.
writer: The workbook is written by the app, not by a library. A stored zip and five XML parts, about 160 lines, so it works on a tablet in a hangar with no signal. Checked both ways: the file reads back byte-identical through the app's own reader, and opens clean in a strict spreadsheet parser.
language: Every British spelling and idiom taken out. "Aircraft" is now "aircraft" in all 86 places it appeared, and with it labour/labor, colour/color, authorisation/authorization, recognised/recognized, digitised/digitized, grey/gray, carburettor/carburetor, neighbour/neighbor, cancelled/canceled and the rest. Two idioms went with them: a "fortnight" is now a two-week window, and the legacy-directive note that told a mechanic which fortnight to look in now says which two-week issue. Nobody on a US ramp says aircraft.
portal: The owner's status page is served from the snapshot the app publishes, and that snapshot no longer contains photographs — only links to them, in the same bucket folder the report and invoice already use. The portal needed no change to read it: a photograph has always been {url: ...} and only what the url points at is different, which is why every job published before 3.390.0 still renders. Unpublishing already deleted that whole folder, so nothing is left on the open web that was not before.
board: The shop board reads shop_board_read() and is written by shop_board_push(), both in migration 020 and extended by 022. Neither has been run against production yet. Until they are, this app's push fails silently and the board says in plain English that it is not switched on — which is the behaviour both sides were built for. The job id on the board is this app's own file id, so a board row and a tablet file are the same thing under two names, and the deep link needs no lookup table.
offline: The dashboard works with no signal, which is the whole reason this was worth doing carefully. Every good answer from the server is written to the tablet, and with no bars the last one is drawn with the date it was true stamped across the top — "Showing the shop as it was 3 days ago" — rather than a spinner or an error. The clock is NOT frozen at the moment of the last sync: an invoice has to keep getting more overdue while the signal is out, or the screen would quietly stop ageing and tell a comfortable lie. A tablet that has never reached the dashboard says so plainly instead of drawing an empty shop.
how_it_was_merged: The board's stylesheet and the app's both use .panel, .row, .top, .brand and .mark, so dropping one on the other would have wrecked both. Every board selector is scoped to #dashView by a brace-matching pass rather than a regex — a regex over CSS gets the media queries wrong and you find out on somebody's telephone — and the board's custom properties moved from :root onto #dashView itself, so inside the dashboard they win and everywhere else the app's own values are untouched. Of 911 app element ids and 91 board ones there was exactly one collision, and it was inside a screen that got deleted. The board spoke to Supabase through its browser library; the app talks to the same database over plain REST with its own token handling. One twelve-line adapter sits between them, so not a single call site had to change.
